title: OPPOSITION: SONO (003248587)
text:
OPPOSITION DIVISION
OPPOSITION Nо B 3 248 587
Sono Tecnologia Audiovisual, S.L., Pogrés, 29 Pol. Ind. Almeda, 08940 Cornellà de
Llobregat (Barcelona), Spain (opponent), represented by Isern Patentes y Marcas, S.L.,
Avenida Diagonal, 463 bis, 2° piso, 08036 Barcelona, Spain (professional representative)
a g a i n s t
Blooming Grace Co., Ltd., 12, Dosan-daero 81-gil, Gangnam-gu, 06011 Seoul, South
Korea (holder), represented by Rolf Sander, Birger Jarlsgatan 99a, 11356 Stockholm,
Sweden (professional representative).
On 30/07/2026, the Opposition Division takes the following
DECISION:
1. Opposition No B 3 248 587 is upheld for all the contested goods and services.
2. International registration No 1 857 008 is entirely refused protection in respect of the
European Union.
3. The holder bears the costs, fixed at EUR 620.
REASONS
On 03/10/2025, the opponent filed an opposition against all the goods and services of
international registration designating the European Union No 1 857 008 ‘SONO’ (word
mark). The opposition is based on, inter alia, Spanish trade mark registration No 2 734 401
(figurative mark). The opponent invoked Article 8(1)(b) EUTMR.
LIKELIHOOD OF CONFUSION — ARTICLE 8(1)(b) EUTMR
Pursuant to Article 8(1)(b) EUTMR, a likelihood of confusion exists if there is a risk that the
public might believe that the goods or services in question, under the assumption that they
bear the marks in question, come from the same undertaking or, as the case may be, from
economically linked undertakings. Whether a likelihood of confusion exists depends on the
appreciation in a global assessment of several factors, which are interdependent. These
factors include the similarity of the signs, the similarity of the goods and services, the
distinctiveness of the earlier mark, the distinctive and dominant elements of the conflicting
signs, and the relevant public.
The opposition is based on more than one earlier trade mark. The Opposition Division finds
it appropriate to first examine the opposition in relation to the opponent’s Spanish trade mark
registration No 2 734 401.

Decision on Opposition No B 3 248 587 Page 2 of 7
a) The goods and services
The goods and services on which the opposition is based are the following:
Class 9: Scientific, nautical, geodesic, photographic, cinematographic, optical and teaching
apparatus and instruments; apparatus and instruments for conducting, switching,
transforming, accumulating, regulating or controlling electricity; apparatus for the registration,
transmission, reproduction of sound or images; phonograph records; automatic vending
machines and mechanisms for coin-operated apparatus; cash registers, calculating
machines, data processing equipment and computers; fire extinguishers; computer readers,
magnetic stripe recorders, computer peripheral devices, computers, printers for use with
computers, computer memories, recorded computer programs, downloadable computer
programs, procesadores, processors (central processing units), data processing equipment;
software, recorded computer operating programs; magnetic data media; CD roms; floppy
disks; DVD's.
Class 35: Organization of exhibitions for commercial or advertising purposes; sales
promotion for others; projects (business management assistance); public relations services;
retail sales in shops and through worldwide computer networks; advertising; business
management; business administration; import and export services; services in support of the
operation or management of a commercial enterprise on a franchising basis; professional
business consultancy; book-keeping; advisory services for business management; statistical
information; market studies; provision of business information; market research; business
appraisals; business expertise; opinion polling; magazine press services; advertising
information services; rental of advertising space; publicity material rental; rental of
advertising time in any media; dissemination of advertising matter; direct mail advertising
(leaflets, brochures, printed matter, samples); radio advertising; television advertising;
advertising by mail order; on-line advertising on a computer network; organization of
exhibitions for commercial or advertising purposes; business management assistance.
Class 41: Education, training and leisure services, sporting and cultural activities; arranging
and conducting of congresses, conferences, courses, seminars, symposiums, colloquiums;
organization of exhibitions for cultural or educational purposes and museum services
(presentations and exhibitions); publication of texts, other than publicity texts
Class 42: Scientific and technological services, as well as research and design services
relating thereto; industrial analysis and research services, computer design and
development, computer consultancy, software design and development, computer
consultancy, professional consultancy and advice included in this class; hosting services,
creation, design and maintenance of web pages for third parties, superserver (web pages),
recovery of computer data; conducting technical project studies
The contested goods and services are the following:
Class 9: Phonograph records; audio recordings featuring music; downloadable musical
sound recordings; digital music downloadable from the Internet; optical discs featuring
music; pre-recorded DVDs featuring music; downloadable music files; downloadable digital
video recordings; prerecorded motion picture videos; downloadable multimedia file;
downloadable digital content in the form of electronic publications of brochures;
downloadable tickets; computer software for organizing and viewing digital images and
photographs.
Class 41: Arranging and conducting of concerts; presentation of live performances; provision
of information relating to entertainment, music, live performances and entertainment events;
entertainment services provided by performing artists; entertainment services in the form of

Decision on Opposition No B 3 248 587 Page 3 of 7
concert performances; organization of shows for cultural purposes; rental of audio
recordings via internet online; providing information in the field of entertainment; fan club
services in the nature of entertainment; arranging and conducting of entertainment events;
digital video, audio and multimedia entertainment publishing services; production of sound
recordings.
The relevant factors relating to the comparison of the goods or services include, inter alia,
their nature, their intended purpose, their method of use and whether they are in competition
with each other or are complementary (‘the Canon criteria’). It is also necessary to take into
account, besides the Canon criteria, other factors, namely distribution channels, the relevant
public and the usual origin of the goods or services (02/06/2021, T‑177/20, Hispano Suiza /
Hispano Suiza, EU:T:2021:312, § 21-22).
Contested goods in Class 9
The contested phonograph records are identically contained in both lists of goods.
The contested audio recordings featuring music include, as a broader category, the
opponent’s phonograph records. Since the Opposition Division cannot dissect ex officio the
broad category of the contested goods, they are considered identical to the opponent’s
goods.
The contested optical discs featuring music are included in the broad category of, or overlap
with the opponent's CD roms. Therefore, they are identical.
The contested pre-recorded DVDs featuring music; prerecorded motion picture videos are
included in, or overlap with the broad category of the opponent's DVD’s. Therefore, they are
identical.
The contested computer software for organizing and viewing digital images and photographs
are included in the broad category of the opponent's recorded computer programs.
Therefore, they are identical.
The contested downloadable musical sound recordings; digital music downloadable from the
Internet; downloadable music files are similar to the opponent's phonograph records
because they coincide in purpose and are in competition. They target the same public to
whom they are offered by the same producer.
The contested downloadable digital content in the form of electronic publications of
brochures is similar to the opponent's magnetic data media because they coincide in
distribution channels, relevant public, and producer. Furthermore, they are complementary.
The contested downloadable digital video recordings; downloadable multimedia file are
similar to a low degree to the opponent's magnetic data media because they coincide
distribution channels, and relevant public. Furthermore, they are complementary.
The contested downloadable tickets are similar to a low degree to the opponent's
organization of exhibitions for cultural or educational purposes and museum services
(presentations and exhibitions) in Class 41 because they coincide in distribution channels
and relevant public. Furthermore, they are complementary.
Contested services in Class 41

Decision on Opposition No B 3 248 587 Page 4 of 7
The contested arranging and conducting of concerts; presentation of live performances;
organization of shows for cultural purposes are included in the broad category of, or overlap
with, the opponent's cultural activities. Therefore, they are identical.
The contested multimedia entertainment publishing services overlap with the opponent's
publication of texts, other than publicity texts. Therefore, they are identical.
The contested provision of information relating to entertainment, music, live performances
and entertainment events; entertainment services provided by performing artists;
entertainment services in the form of concert performances; rental of audio recordings via
internet online; providing information in the field of entertainment; fan club services in the
nature of entertainment; arranging and conducting of entertainment events are at least
similar to the opponent's leisure services, since they coincide in distribution channels,
relevant public and provider.
The contested digital video, audio entertainment publishing services similar to the
opponent's education services since they can coincide distribution channels, relevant public
and provider. Furthermore, they are complementary.
The contested production of sound recordings are similar to the opponent’s phonograph
records in Class 9, since they can coincide in purpose, relevant public and producer.
b) Relevant public — degree of attention
The average consumer of the category of products concerned is deemed to be reasonably
well informed and reasonably observant and circumspect. It should also be borne in mind
that the average consumer’s degree of attention is likely to vary according to the category of
goods or services in question (22/06/1999, C-342/97, Lloyd Schuhfabrik, EU:C:1999:323, §
26).
In the present case, the goods and services found to be identical and similar to varying
degrees target the public at large as well as business customers with specific professional
knowledge or expertise.
The degree of attention is average.
c) The signs
SONO
Earlier trade mark Contested sign
The relevant territory is Spain.
The global appreciation of the visual, aural or conceptual similarity of the marks in question
must be based on the overall impression given by the marks, bearing in mind, in particular,
their distinctive and dominant components (11/11/1997, C‑251/95, Sabèl, EU:C:1997:528,
§ 23).
The sole verbal element 'SONO' of the both signs will be perceived by the Spanish-speaking
public as a coined or fanciful term. Although the root 'son-' appears in Spanish words such

Decision on Opposition No B 3 248 587 Page 5 of 7
as 'sonido' (sound) and 'sonoro' (sonorous), 'sono' as a standalone term is not a standard
Spanish dictionary word and does not carry a precise, immediately understood meaning.
Therefore, it is distinctive to a normal degree.
In the earlier mark ‘SONO is written in standard bold red characters, and the signs further
contains a figurative element made up of six short horizontal black lines arranged vertically.
These figurative features are merely decorative and devoid of distinctive character. Finally, it
should be noted that neither element is visually more striking than the other. Yet, when signs
consist of both verbal and figurative components, in principle, the verbal component of the
sign usually has a stronger impact on the consumer than the figurative component. This is
because the public does not tend to analyse signs and will more easily refer to the signs in
question by their verbal element than by describing their figurative elements (14/07/2005, T-
312/03, SELENIUM-ACE / SELENIUM SPEZIAL A-C-E (fig.), EU:T:2005:289, § 37).
Visually, the signs coincide in the verbal element 'SONO'. They only differ in the figurative
features the earlier mark which are, however, merely decorative. Therefore, the signs are
visually similar to a high degree.
Aurally, the pronunciation of the signs coincides fully in the sounds of the letters 'S-O-N-O',
present identically in both signs. Therefore, the signs are aurally identical.
Conceptually, neither of the signs has a meaning for the public in the relevant territory.
Since a conceptual comparison is not possible, the conceptual aspect does not influence the
assessment of the similarity of the signs.
As the signs have been found similar in at least one aspect of the comparison, the
examination of likelihood of confusion will proceed.
d) Distinctiveness of the earlier mark
The distinctiveness of the earlier mark is one of the factors to be taken into account in the
global assessment of likelihood of confusion.
The opponent did not explicitly claim that its mark is particularly distinctive by virtue of
intensive use or reputation.
Consequently, the assessment of the distinctiveness of the earlier mark will rest on its
distinctiveness per se. In the present case, the earlier trade mark as a whole has no
meaning for any of the goods and services in question from the perspective of the public in
the relevant territory. Therefore, the distinctiveness of the earlier mark must be seen as
normal.
e) Global assessment, other arguments and conclusion
The goods and services are identical and similar to varying degrees and they target the
public at large as well as business customers with specific professional knowledge or
expertise, whose degree of attention is average. The earlier mark has a normal degree of
distinctiveness. While the conceptual aspect plays no role in the overall comparison, the
signs are visually similar to a high degree and aurally identical.
Account is taken of the fact that average consumers rarely have the chance to make a direct
comparison between different marks but must trust in their imperfect recollection of them
(22/06/1999, C‑342/97, Lloyd Schuhfabrik, EU:C:1999:323, § 26).

Decision on Opposition No B 3 248 587 Page 6 of 7
Even consumers who pay a high degree of attention need to rely on their imperfect
recollection of trade marks (21/11/2013, T‑443/12, ancotel. (fig.) / ACOTEL (fig.) et al.,
EU:T:2013:605, § 54).
Likelihood of confusion covers situations where the consumer directly confuses the trade
marks themselves, or where the consumer makes a connection between the conflicting
signs and assumes that the goods/services covered are from the same or economically
linked undertakings (29/09/1998, C‑39/97, Canon, EU:C:1998:442, § 29). Indeed, it is highly
conceivable that the relevant consumer will perceive the contested mark as a sub-brand, a
variation of the earlier mark, configured in a different way according to the type of goods or
services that it designates (23/10/2002, T‑104/01, Fifties / Miss Fifties (fig.), EU:T:2002:262,
§ 49).
Considering all the above, there is a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public.
Therefore, the opposition is well founded on the basis of the opponent’s Spanish trade mark
registration No M2 734 401. It follows that the contested trade mark must be rejected for all
the contested goods and services.
As the earlier right No M2 734 401 ‘SONO’ leads to the success of the opposition and to the
rejection of the contested trade mark for all the goods and services against which the
opposition was directed, there is no need to examine the other earlier rights invoked by the
opponent (16/09/2004, T-342/02, Moser Grupo Media, s.l. (fig.) / MGM, EU:T:2004:268).
COSTS
According to Article 109(1) EUTMR, the losing party in opposition proceedings must bear the
fees and costs incurred by the other party.
Since the holder is the losing party, it must bear the opposition fee as well as the costs
incurred by the opponent in the course of these proceedings.
According to Article 109(1) and (7) EUTMR and Article 18(1)(c)(i) EUTMIR, the costs to be
paid to the opponent are the opposition fee and the costs of representation, which are to be
fixed on the basis of the maximum rate set therein.
The Opposition Division
Martina GALLE Monika CISZEWSKA Réka MÉSZÁROS
According to Article 67 EUTMR, any party adversely affected by this decision has a right to
appeal against this decision. According to Article 68 EUTMR, notice of appeal must be filed
in writing at the Office within two months of the date of notification of this decision. It must be
filed in the language of the proceedings in which the decision subject to appeal was taken.
Furthermore, a written statement of the grounds for appeal must be filed within four months

of the same date. The notice of appeal will be deemed to have been filed only when the
appeal fee of EUR 720 has been paid.
